title: Cheapest Route With Backward Roads
statement:
A town has n junctions numbered 0 to n − 1 and a list of one-way roads, where [u, v, w] lets you drive from u to v for cost w.

Every junction also has a one-time switch. While you stand at junction u, you may use its switch to flip one road that points into u (some [v, u, w]) and drive it right away from u to v, paying 2w. Each junction's switch works only once.

Return the cheapest total cost to get from junction 0 to junction n − 1, or -1 if it cannot be done.

examples.why: Drive 0 → 1 (3). At junction 1, flip the road 2 → 1 and drive it backwards (2 · 1 = 2). Then 2 → 3 (4).
The direct road costs 30. Driving both other roads backwards costs 8 + 12 = 20, even at double price.
No road touches junction 2 at all.

hints: Ignore the "once per junction" rule for a moment. What does the switch let you do in graph terms?
It adds, for every road v → u of cost w, a road u → v of cost 2w. A cheapest route never visits a junction twice, so it never needs a switch twice.
Build that doubled graph and run Dijkstra from 0.

explain.intuition:
The switch at u only matters at the moment you stand on u, and it lets you leave along any road that points into u, backwards, at double cost. So model it as extra edges: for each road v → u with cost w, add u → v with cost 2w.

What about "only once per junction"? With positive costs, a cheapest route never visits the same junction twice: cutting out the loop would only make it cheaper. So each junction is left at most once, and its switch is used at most once anyway. The limit never bites, and the problem is a plain shortest path with non-negative weights: Dijkstra with a min-heap, like finding the fastest chain of network hops when some links cost extra in one direction.
steps: Build an adjacency list: for each road [u, v, w] add u → v with w and v → u with 2w.
Run Dijkstra from 0: a heap of (dist, node), skip stale entries, relax each neighbour.
Stop when n − 1 is popped and return its distance.
If the heap empties first, return -1.
pitfalls: Adding the reverse edge with cost w instead of 2w, which turns it into an undirected graph.
Trying to track which switches are used in the state. It is correct but blows up the state space for nothing.
Running plain BFS. The edges have different costs, so fewest roads is not cheapest.

solutions.title: Bellman–Ford on the doubled graph
solutions.idea: Relax every forward and backward edge repeatedly until nothing improves.

solutions.title: Dijkstra with reversed edges at double cost
solutions.idea: The once-per-junction limit never binds on a cheapest route, so add every reversed road at 2w and run Dijkstra.

followups: Now the whole trip may use at most k switches in total. How does the state change?
Costs may be 0. Does the argument that each switch is used at most once still hold?
lcTitle: Minimum Cost Path with Edge Reversals
